catalog_quote: 2.3 STRESS The rules for stress assignment are identical to those for Wargamay: (1) if the first syllable involves a long vowel, then it must receive primary stress; (2) if there is no long vowel in a word, and (a) the word is disyllabic or quadrisyllabic, primary stress goes on the first syllable; (b) the word is trisyllabic or quinquesyllabic, primary stress goes on the second syllable. Secondary stress goes on the syllable next but one after primary stress, except that a final syllable can never bear stress. Thus: (1) ŋú:ḏu 'fish (generic)' ḏí:baɽi 'south' (2)(a) ḏíŋa 'man' bíyaḏàla 'water snake' (b) bulbíri 'quail' Also as in Wargamay, a non-initial vowel which bears stress may be phonetically lengthened e.g. [bulbíˑri]; this must be carefully distinguished from the phonologically contrastive length in initial syllables (which has stronger and more consistent quantitative realisatio…

sources.quote: Same two rules verbatim (initial long vowel takes primary stress; else 1st syllable in 2/4-syllable words, 2nd syllable in 3/5-syllable words; secondary on the next-but-one syllable, never final). Adds: 'stress shifts between the absolutive form of a noun ... and an oblique form, e.g. múŋan mountain-ABS, muŋán-da mountain-LOC'; 'The Wargamay stress assignment rules make it impossible to get two successive stressed syllables'; ordered derivation: phonological length -> stress rule -> optional phonetic lengthening of non-initial stressed syllable.

sources.citation: Bundle cites the same primary (Dixon 1983 'Nyawaygi', HAL vol.3 [StressTyp2 mis-cites vol.2]) plus secondary/theoretical Hayes 1995:180 ('Nyawaygi has the same stress pattern as neighbouring Wargamay') and Hayes 1995:140 (Wargamay rule), and Bailey 1995 (no text). No different primary description is cited.
